ch21.note: Shanghai's river geography: ships leave the Yangtze estuary and turn into the Huangpu River at the Wusong (Woosung) rivermouth below the city. The Huangpu's west bank held the foreign wharves and the Bund, the grand waterfront of the concessions; Pudong, the east bank, was the low industrial shore opposite.

ch21.anchor: an amah who kept the house
ch21.note: An amah was a live-in maidservant—the word passed into treaty-port English from southern Chinese. A safe house kept up with a cook and an amah passed for the household of an ordinary well-off family, which was exactly the cover wanted.

ch21.anchor: Mr. Dai was himself a man of Jiangshan
ch21.note: Jiangshan, a county in Zhejiang, was Dai Li's birthplace. Trusting native-place ties above all, he filled his most confidential posts—couriers, cooks, housekeepers of safe houses—with fellow Jiangshan men and women, so that 'a Jiangshan person' recurs as shorthand for one of Dai's own.

In the 'solitary island' years, when the foreign concessions stood unoccupied amid Japanese-held Shanghai, the city's cabarets and dance halls stayed open till dawn. Their crowds and anonymity made them a place an agent could pass the small hours when a hotel or a home had become too dangerous.
